title: Scientists discover a rare stellar fossil that preserves clues to the universe's first generations of stars
body_text: Astronomers have discovered a rare ancient star, HE 1153−0518, whose chemical composition preserves the signatures of some of the earliest generations of stars in the Universe. The earliest generations of stars in the Universe formed only a few hundred million years after the Big Bang. Although those massive stars no longer exist, they enriched the primordial gas with newly synthesized elements before ending their lives in supernovae explosions. Ancient metal-poor stars that formed from this enriched gas preserve these chemical signatures and therefore act as "stellar fossils," allowing astronomers to reconstruct the history of the early Universe. Hence the discovery of such a rare stellar fossil provides important clues to the nucleosynthesis processes that enriched the primordial Universe and shaped the chemical evolution of our Galaxy. Using high-resolution spectroscopic data collected at Subaru telescope at Hawaii, together with recent astrometric and photometric data, a team from the Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA), Bengaluru, an Autonomous Institute of the Department of Science and Technology (DST) and Dakshin Kamrup College, Assam, determined the atmospheric properties and chemical abundances of the star with high precision. These measurements of atmospheric properties and chemical abundances enable a comprehensive investigation of the nucleosynthetic history of how its various elements were synthesized in nuclear reactions and its evolutionary status. Fig : Yoon-Beers diagram showing the absolute carbon abundance, A(C), as a function of metallicity, [Fe/H], for carbon-enhanced metal-poor (CEMP) stars.  The coloured ellipses show the approximate locations of the different groups as indicated. The large yellow star marks HE 1153-0518 from this work.  The solid black line represents the CEMP classification boundary corresponding to [C/Fe] = +0.7. The study identifies HE 1153−0518 as a previously unknown sub-class of carbon-enhanced metal-poor (CEMP) stars called CEMP-no star. Among the CEMP stars, CEMP-no stars form a sub-group that exhibits enhancement in carbon and is deficient in heavy elements. These stars form a rare class of stellar fossils that provides a direct window into the earliest phases of Galactic evolution. The star HE 1153-0518 contains only about one-thousandth of the Sun's iron abundance, yet is remarkably rich in carbon and sodium while being severely deficient in heavy elements produced by neutron-capture nucleosynthesis. The study also measures a low carbon isotopic ( 12 C/ 13 C) ratio, indicating that the star has experienced significant internal mixing of its gas. Its spectral energy distribution in the optical and infrared wavebands reveals evidence of excess infrared emission, suggesting the possible presence of circumstellar dust. Together, these observational characteristics provide valuable insights into both the intrinsic evolution of the star and the chemical environment from which it formed. "Ancient metal-poor stars are among the oldest surviving objects in our Galaxy. They formed from gas that had been enriched by the very first stellar explosions. Their chemical composition allows us to investigate nucleosynthesis that occurred more than 13 billion years ago. Discoveries such as HE 1153−0518 bring us closer to understanding how the first generations of stars enriched the universe with the elements that later became the building blocks of stars, planets and life.” explained Aruna Goswami of the Indian IIA and a co-author of the study. To understand the origin of the observed abundance pattern, the authors compare the measured elemental abundances with predictions from theoretical nucleosynthesis models. Partha Pratim Goswami, from Dakshin Kamrup College and the lead author of the study, explains the broader significance of the discovery: "Every newly discovered chemically primitive star helps us reconstruct the earliest history of the Milky Way and the lives of the first stars. These stellar fossils provide some of the strongest observational constraints on models of stellar nucleosynthesis and Galactic chemical evolution." This discovery published in journal the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society (MNRAS), expands the growing inventory of stellar fossils that preserve the chemical record of the early Universe. The study demonstrates how high-resolution stellar spectroscopy continues to uncover relics of the early Milky Way, a field of study that has long been pursued at the Indian Institute of Astrophysics, an autonomous institution under the Department of Science and Technology, Government of India. By decoding the elemental compositions of ancient stars, astronomers can investigate events that occurred more than 13 billion years ago, well before the formation of the Sun and the Solar System.
